newsitem.title: INDIA: India raises investment limit for foreign funds.
newsitem.headline: India raises investment limit for foreign funds.

text.p: India on Friday raised the limit on foreign institutional investors' equity stakes in domestic companies to 30 percent from 24 percent in a move expected to attract foreign portfolio funds in stocks.
In a statement, the government said a decision to raise the ceiling, announced in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget presented to parliament on February 28, had been implemented.
"The government has notified enhancement of limits on investments by foreign financial investors (FIIs) from 24 percent to 30 percent," the statement said.

The government implemented the change despite a political crisis threatening the future of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who faces a vote of confidence in parliament on April 11 after the Congress Party withdrew make-or-break support.
Congress withdrew its support on Sunday, leaving Deve Gowda's minority government to prove it has the support to pass the trust vote in the 545-member lower of house of parliament.
The 15-member ruling coalition controls 180 votes, Congress 140 and the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party and allies 193.
Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition government is sending strong signals to foreign investors and domestic industry on its intention to go ahead with key economic decisions, business leaders said.

"The government wants to show that they are setting the budgetary proposals in motion. Economics is moving ahead inspite of political uncertainty," V. Raghuraman, secretary-general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters.

Under the new guidelines, FIIs, non-resident (expatriate) Indians and overseas commercial bodies (OCBs) or investment firms set up by expatriates will together be able to hold up to 30 percent of an Indian firm's capital.
But companies that want to allow FIIs to increase their holdings beyond 24 percent need to have the proposal approved by their boards of directors and shareholders, officials said.

The government earlier this week announced a new trade policy, valid from 1997-2002 (April-March), that liberalised imports and also eased rules for external commercial borrowings by Indian companies.

"These are steps by this government to steal (the) thunder from the next government, if the Deve Gowda government falls, and show that they are serious about reforms," said Vipin Aggrawal, chief dealer at DBS Capital Trust Securities.
